title: The origins of Scottish brochs

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The word 'broch' derives from the Norse borg, meaning fort, and is used by archaeologists to describe the characteristic circular towers found on, or very near, the coasts of Scotland. Although brochs were built in all areas of the country, few of those in the lowland areas of the south and east have survived. However, they knew that brochs north and west the remains of many brochs can still be seen. Dun Telve, which is near the village of Glenelg opposite the island of Skye, is a good example.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: When historians began to study these structures in the 18th and 19th centuries, they likened them to the defensive towers which were built on the borders with England in the 15th century, as the strongholds of local landowners. However, they knew that brochs were much earlier – perhaps built by the Viking invaders or the native Pictish populations following the departure of the Romans from Britain in the 5th century. But when excavations began in the mid-19th century, they produced a good deal of material that was thought to date from the Roman period. Historians then revised their thinking, and interpreted brochs as a response to Roman slaving expeditions and military activity in the 1st century AD. However, in the 1950s this theory was also undone by the development of reliable radiocarbon-dating techniques. These now show that the number of brochs had been built several centuries before the first Romans arrived in Scotland.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In the lowland parts of Scotland, most brochs were made out of timber, and consequently have not survived, except as crop marks in aerial photographs. These show the position of a ring of posts which – as we know from excavated examples – would have formed the framework for a wattle-and-daub* wall supporting a cone-shaped roof thatched with dried reeds. In northern and western Scotland, timber was a scarce and very valuable resource, so stone was used instead. Many brochs here have survived in various states of preservation, and there are many more sites where identity is unclear because they are either too damaged or have not been properly investigated.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In most cases, the walls of stone brochs are hollow for much of their height, with an inner and outer skin, bound together by horizontal supports. The cavities are known as galleries, and were normally accessible from a staircase which wound at least part way around the interior of the wall. On the west coast and the Hebridean islands in the north west, the galleries normally extend the whole height of the tower (the so-called 'ground-galleried' type), while in Caithness, Sutherland and the Northern Isles the tendency is towards solid bases with galleries only occurring from the first floor and up. It is thought that the one type evolved out of the other, but there is some disagreement as to which came first. And since neither type is exclusive to its supposed territory, it may be that there is some other explanation for the distinction. In many instances there were no other openings apart from the long entrance passage – no level or higher, but there were no windows for example. In most cases the interiors have been badly disturbed but where features have survived, these were generally the remains of a central fireplace and partitions around the perimeter of the space. Many brochs also have sacrements – narrow ledges on the inner face of the walls – designed to support the woodwork for a roof or the floor of an upper storey.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The assumption that brochs were fortresses has recently come under question. Many of them are too poorly located to serve as fortifications because they are overlooked by higher ground or have no reliable supply of water. The only broch with a parapet at the top (or even access to the top) is Mousa on Shetland, and none of the brochs have any windows, so mounting an active defence would have been difficult, to say the least. There is also the matter of proximity. The Gurness broch, for example, are only about a kilometre apart and are within full view of one another, and they are in close proximity to one another in Orkney too. At best, they might have served as emergency shelters, but even then a little patience and a good fire would have been all that any attacker needed to smoke out the defenders. It is now widely believed that their true purpose was to advertise the prestige and power of the chieftains who lived in them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In the past, there was also some debate as to whether the brochs were a native idea, or whether they were introduced by invaders, in much the same way as the Normans introduced the moteand-bailey** castle to help them control a hostile countryside. But now it is generally believed that brochs were entirely native structures which developed from the roundhouse tradition. Circular houses had been a distinctive feature of the British landscape at least since the Early Bronze Age, which began early in the second millennium BC, and for well over a thousand years before brochs appeared.
